newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: Protesters gather as PNG crisis simmers on.
newsitem.headline: Protesters gather as PNG crisis simmers on.

text.p: Protesters calling for the reinstatement of Papua New Guinea's sacked army chief gathered in the capital on Friday despite a government climbdown over the use of foreign mercenaries to put down an island uprising.
Around 100 protesters arrived in the early hours at Port Moresby's Murray barracks, where riot police and thousands of looting demonstrators have fought running battles this week.
The PNG capital was otherwise calm as the country's worst political crisis entered its fifth day. Schools were closed and police roadblocks set up on major roads in the run-down city.

But local media reported that the government of Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan was considering imposing a state of emergency on the capital, where an anti-crime curfew has already been in place since late last year.
The city's governor, Bill Skate, appealed for calm. "Looting and rioting are uncalled for and I want every resident in the city to keep calm," Skate said.
Dozens of people were injured in street violence on Thursday and opposition groups said on Friday that five or six were in critical condition. There were no reports of any deaths.

Soliders, who have remained in their barracks during the unrest, were almost caught up in the violence on Thursday when police chased a group of protesters into the Murray barracks and fired tear gas.
While the army has led the opposition to Chan this week, the police force has been backing the prime minister and any confrontation between the two forces would escalate the crisis.
The unrest, the worst since PNG earned independence in 1975, began on Monday when army commander Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok demanded Chan quit over the Sandline deal.
Singirok was promptly sacked but remains in the army barracks and has become the focus for simmering anti-government dissent among poor city residents.
Chan on Thursday announced that a controversial deal with British mercenary company Sandline International was being suspended pending an investigation into the US28 million deal.

The mercenaries, mostly South African apartheid-era veterans and said to number up to 70, have already begun to leave PNG. Their planned operation to use helicopter gunships to quash a nine-year rebellion on Bougainville island was thwarted by the troops they were meant to be fighting alongside.
British diplomats were trying to track down the mercenaries' commander, retired British army colonel Tim Spicer, a former U.N. peacekeeper in Bosnia who now heads Sandline.
Spicer was being detained by rebel PNG soldiers along with the other mercenaries and a PNG army major said on Thursday Spicer would be the last mercenary out of the country.
Australia welcomed Chan's suspension of the mercenary contract and urged the immediate departure of the hired guns to help restore peace to the South Pacific nation.
"I hope to see Sandline on aircraft out of Papua New Guinea -- and as soon as possible," Foreign Minister Alexander Downer told Australian radio.
Australia's top diplomat, despatched to Port Moresby to help resolve the crisis, was due to resume talks with Chan on Friday.
Australia was the colonial administrator of Papua New Guinea until 1975 and retains close ties as the country's largest source of aid and investment.
Canberra has offered "practical alternatives" to the use of mercenaries, thought to involve increased training for the ill-equipped and poorly-trained Papua New Guinea military.
